retrieval_text: A 32-year-old female presented with a red, swollen plaque on the inner side of her left forearm, which had been present for 10 days. She experienced general discomfort before the appearance of the lesion, followed by itching and a burning sensation at the site. Initially small, the lesion grew to approximately 5 cm by 4 cm. The plaque started as pink-red and changed to a violet color over 10 days, eventually fading within 3 weeks and leaving slight darkening of the skin. She reported having had 15 similar episodes over the past 18 months, with the lesion recurring at the same location and accompanied by mild general symptoms. The severity of these episodes varied, sometimes necessitating the use of antihistamines and oral steroids for relief.
A 71-year-old right-handed man with a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and glaucoma experienced progressive stiffness in his right arm and speech difficulties over one year.

A 12-year-old boy was bitten by a southern Pacific rattlesnake (Crotalus oreganus helleri) near the lateral malleolus while walking past a tarp in his uncle's garage in southern California. He described the pain in his foot as intense, comparing it to being 'lit on fire and run over by a truck.' The snake was found and identified by a local herpetologist. Initial treatment in the emergency department included intravenous opioids for pain management, CroFab® antivenom [Crotalidae polyvalent immune Fab (ovine)], and fluid hydration.

A 2.5-year-old boy was seen at the Dentistry Department of Pediatric Dentistry Faculty, Shiraz University of Medical Sciences, in June 2011. He exhibited early loss of the mandibular primary canines and the maxillary right primary canine. Clinical examination showed absence of all maxillary and mandibular primary incisors. According to his parents, the primary incisors had not yet emerged. Extraoral examination noted lip eversion and fine hair, with normal eyebrows and eyelashes. There were no issues with heat intolerance or sweating. The toenails were observed to be spoon-shaped and underdeveloped. A panoramic view was not obtained due to the child's lack of cooperation. Examination of the parents' oral health showed normal dentition and no abnormalities in nails, scalp, hair, or eyebrows. There was no family history of similar conditions, except for a cleft palate in one of the maternal cousins.

A 24-year-old male Caucasian presented with secondary hypertension that began at age eleven. Despite treatment with four antihypertensive medications (AT1-receptor antagonist, β-blocker, calcium channel antagonist, and doxazosin mesylate), his blood pressure remained high. Initial examination showed a blood pressure of 180/95 mmHg and a heart rate of 82 beats per minute. A 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure measurement while on treatment indicated an average blood pressure of 183/98 mmHg with a heart rate of 71 bpm, with no nocturnal dip. Other physical findings were normal. Serum electrolytes were: sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, calcium 2.7 mmol/L, inorganic phosphorus 4.1 mg/dL, and magnesium 1.97 mg/dL. Renal, liver, and thyroid tests were normal.

A 24-year-old male presented with a 15-day history of persistent swelling of the upper lip that ulcerated 2 days prior. He reported no history of trauma, fever, cough, weight loss, or drug or tobacco usage, and his past medical and dental history was non-contributory. The patient was thin built with normal vital signs and no lymphadenopathy. Examination revealed a diffuse, non-tender swelling of the lower lip with mild eversion. A reddish-pink granular lesion was observed involving the vermillion border, labial mucosa, floor of the mouth, and mandibular anterior gingiva. The lesion exhibited patchy areas of brown crustation, bleeding, and purulent discharge.

A 57-year-old male from Monte Dourado, PA, Brazil, was referred for neurological evaluation in Belém, PA, Brazil, due to brachiocrural paresis that had been progressing over three years. Initially, symptoms were noted in the lower limbs, and after one year, the upper limbs also exhibited paresis, along with fasciculations and tremors in the extremities. Subsequently, the patient experienced dysarthria, dysphagia, and sexual dysfunction. Thirty years prior, he had undergone surgery for gynecomastia. Neurological examination revealed impaired gait, inability to walk on tiptoes, proximal muscle atrophy in the upper limbs, and fasciculations in both upper and lower limbs. Reflex testing showed bilateral hyporeflexia in the triceps, biceps, brachioradialis, pronator, and patellar reflexes (grade 1 on the deep tendon reflexes grading scale), with absent Achilles reflexes bilaterally (grade 0). Muscle strength was graded as 4 in the bilateral lower limbs and proximal upper limbs according to the Medical Research Council (MRC) scale. Bulbar involvement was noted with uvula deviation to the right during phonation and tongue atrophy with fasciculations. Surgical scars from the gynecomastia correction were present.
A 75-year-old Japanese man presented with sudden, asymptomatic gross hematuria.

The patient is a 13-month-old male of Chinese descent who was referred for genetic evaluation due to recurrent fever. He is the only child of healthy, non-consanguineous parents with no family history of genetic diseases. Pregnancy was uncomplicated, and no abnormalities were noted at birth. At 7 months old, the patient experienced recurrent fever (8 episodes within two months) with a maximum temperature of 39.2°C and a persistent upper respiratory tract infection. A small facial rash appeared following the fever. Physical examination was otherwise unremarkable, with no palpable lymph nodes.
A 44-year-old woman experienced recurring pain in the right side of her lower jaw for six years.
A 48-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 2-month history of recurrent abdominal pain, which had worsened over the past 2 weeks.

A 19-year-old female presented with pain in the mandibular anterior region for the past 2 days. She is one of two siblings from non-consanguineous parents, with no family history of orofacial or acral malformations. Her antenatal, neonatal, and infancy periods were uneventful. At the age of 7, she underwent surgical management for an atrial septal defect. She reported menstrual irregularities, with menarche occurring at age 16. She is moderately built, well-nourished, and appears to have normal intelligence. Her height is 167 cm (75th percentile), while her weight (42 kg) and head circumference (20 inches) are both below the 3rd percentile. General physical examination showed broad halluces bilaterally with valgus deformity and dysmorphic nails. There is duplication of the 5th toe on the right foot with syndactyly of the supernumerary digit with the 5th toe. Flexion contraction of the 4th and 5th toes on the left foot and the 4th toe on the right foot was noted. The upper limbs are normal except for a broadened right thumb and nail, and bilateral clinodactyly. No functional deficits in the hands or feet were observed. Extra-oral examination revealed an acrocephalic skull, flattened frontal and occipital regions, and a low hairline. The patient has a leptoprosopic flat face with mild maxillary hypoplasia, relative mandibular prognathism, and a prominent chin. An increased gonial angle was noted on profile view. The nose is long, thin, and pointed with a flattened nasofrontal angle, presenting as a wide root of the nose. Thick eyebrows, prominent eyelashes, mild convergent strabismus, and marginal hypertelorism were observed. Intra-oral examination showed a high arched palate and generalized enamel hypoplasia. The patient is currently undergoing orthodontic treatment for arch crowding and has an anterior deep bite with 100% overlap of mandibular teeth. She has a history of endodontic treatment and apicoectomy of teeth 31 and 41, and currently reports pain in the same region along with vestibular obliteration and tenderness.

A 17-year-old male presented with painful and tender diffuse erythema and swelling, accompanied by a necrotic lesion on the scrotum for three days. One week prior to these symptoms, he had visited the emergency room with fever and sore throat and was prescribed oral amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid. Physical examination revealed a well-demarcated necrotic lesion approximately 2 cm in size on the anterior scrotum. The lesion was confined to the scrotum, and there was no crepitus in the inflamed tissues. The patient reported no history of local trauma, sexual activity, or other predisposing factors.

A 39-year-old Caucasian male visited our outpatient clinic with seven painless, non-itchy papules that developed within a recent tattoo. These papules emerged approximately three weeks after the patient received a large tattoo on the front side of his right thigh. Initially, the lesions exhibited rapid growth, which later stabilized. Upon physical examination, the papules were found to be unilateral, erythematous, and dome-shaped, with sizes ranging from 4 mm to 1 cm in diameter. Five of the seven lesions were located within the red-inked area of the tattoo, while the remaining two were within the black/gray-inked area. Most of the papules had a thin crust on their surface. The patient reported no previous medical conditions and no additional symptoms. He had received multiple tattoos in the past without any issues and reported no recent sun exposure.

A 23-year-old male army officer visited the clinic with complaints of decreased visual acuity in his left eye over the past 5 months. He had no prior history of eye diseases or surgeries and reported no symptoms such as itching, redness, photophobia, or tearing.

The patient is a 17-year-old Caucasian female who began experiencing upper extremity symptoms at 10.5 years old. Initially, she had mild difficulty extending the left index finger, which progressed to include the right middle finger after one year. By age 12, she developed more noticeable hand weakness, predominantly on the left side. The weakness worsened in cold weather, and her hands were often cold and sweaty. No sensory deficits were observed. There was no history of cervical trauma, but she experienced a growth spurt in the year before symptom onset, growing approximately 8 cm (between the 75th and 90th percentile for growth velocity). There was no family history of neuromuscular disorders. A neurological examination at age 13 revealed significant weakness (MRC 2 to 3−) in the extension of the index and middle fingers bilaterally and in the abduction of the left thumb. There was also weakness (MRC 3+ to 4) in the extension of the ring and little fingers bilaterally, abduction of the right thumb, and abduction and adduction of the left fingers II-V, as well as flexion of the left fingers II-V. Postural tremor and poly-mini-myoclonus of the fingers on extension were observed. There was marked wasting of the right thenar and mild wasting of other intrinsic hand muscles. Muscle strength in wrist flexion and extension, pronation, and supination of the forearms, flexion and extension of the elbow, and shoulder abduction was normal. Sensory deficits were absent, and deep tendon reflexes were intact. Neurological examination of the lower extremities was normal. Cervical spine motility and forward flexion of the whole spine were normal. A motor deficit affecting roots C7 to T1, more pronounced on the left side, was noted. At age 13, her height was 175 cm (5 cm above the 97th percentile), and her weight was 58 kg (75th–90th percentile). By age 14, the pattern of weakness and wasting remained unchanged, though the severity of weakness had slightly increased, stabilizing over the last six months.

A 10-month-old male presented with skin peeling confined to the hands and feet, first observed at 2 months of age. The condition was noted to worsen with exposure to heat and humidity, but not due to mechanical trauma. The patient was born following a normal pregnancy and delivery, with non-consanguineous parents and no relevant family history. Physical examination revealed erythematous erosions with peripheral desquamation on both palms and soles, along with a flaccid blister on the right-hand finger. Mycological tests on the palms and soles returned negative results.

A 5-month-old male, born at full term via cesarean section to nonconsanguineous parents, was admitted due to developmental delays. The mother had taken antiabortion medication early in the pregnancy. There was no family history of developmental delays or seizures. At 5 months, the child was unable to lift his head or roll over. Physical examination revealed wide-set eyes, a high palatal arch, polydactyly of the right little finger, and polydactyly and syndactyly of both little toes. The grandfather had polydactyly of the right hand.

DF, a 64-year-old right-handed male IT technician, began experiencing progressive changes in behavior and emotional stability at the age of 61. Over the next two years, these issues extended to other cognitive areas such as memory and language, with noticeable difficulties in word finding. Additionally, there was an increase in behavioral issues, including excessive oral tendencies and significantly inappropriate actions.

A 36-year-old female patient reported experiencing right ankle pain for the past four years. She had significant weight loss and began physical activity shortly before the onset of symptoms. There was no history of trauma. Initially, she was treated for synovitis with physical therapy, which did not yield significant improvement. She reported paraesthesia along the posterior and medial aspects of the ankle and foot, with symptoms worsening by the end of the day and episodes of cramping in the foot. Physical examination showed a positive dorsiflexion-eversion test that caused numbness in the foot. Tinel's sign was also positive. The range of motion in the ankle was limited due to pain, which was rated 8 on the Visual Analog Score (VAS).
